newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Amazon river port to start shipping soybeans.
newsitem.headline: Amazon river port to start shipping soybeans.

text.p: The floating port of Itacoatiara on Brazil's Amazon river is scheduled to start shipping grains this year and has already programmed 240,000 tonnes of soybeans between April and June, a port official said.
"We have three shipments programmed of 80,000 tonnes each," said superintendent Luiz Antonio Pagot.
Cargill was scheduled to load between April 17 and 22, Andre between May 10 and 20 and Sumitomo between June 10 and 20, Pagot said.
"There is another 70,000 tonnes which has been sold in the export market," he said, adding that the destinations for these cargoes were probably Europe and Asia.

The soybeans are mainly from Sapezal in Mato Grosso state and travel 900 km by land to Porto Velho before covering 1,715 km of river and arriving at Itacotiara, where they are loaded at the floating river terminal.
It is almost the same distance again between Itacotiara and the sea.

The terminal, which only started operating this year, has a capacity of handling three million tonnes of grains per year at a rhythm of 1,500 tonnes per hour, Pagot said. Ships do not berth but are loaded immediately, he added.
The port should reduce freight costs by $50 per tonne for Mato Grosso growers who are currently shipping most of their produce by road, said Tony Fagundes at the Cooperlucas cooperative.
"This would represent a significant saving. We are currently paying $80 per tonne in freight costs," he said.

Local authorities are investing 36 million reais ($34 million) in improving the road linking Cuiaba in Mato Grosso to Santarem, situated on the Amazon river in Para state, he said. There are no rail links to Mato Grosso and Mato Grosso do Sul.
Most of the early-cycle soybeans currently being harvested in the state are destined to crushers rather than ports, Fagundes added.
